title: Spatial Epidemiology, Risk Mapping, and Decision Support Systems
text:
Introduction
This module introduces Geographic Information Systems (GIS) concepts and their applications in health research and infectious disease surveillance. It provides participants with foundational knowledge of spatial data, mapping principles, and the use of tools such as QGIS and R for geospatial analysis.
Participants will gain practical experience in acquiring and cleaning spatial datasets, creating thematic maps, applying cartographic design principles, and performing spatial analyses including buffer analysis, overlay analysis, clustering, and hotspot detection. The module also introduces spatial regression methods and spatial visualization techniques in R.
In addition, participants will learn how to develop interactive dashboards using Shiny App to support visualization, reporting, and decision-making in public health surveillance.






TipExpected Outcome



Participants will be able to generate risk maps, conduct basic spatial analyses, visualize surveillance data geographically, and develop simple dashboards that integrate maps and health indicators to support evidence-based decision-making.

title: Data Collection and Management
text:
This module introduces participants to the full data lifecycle: planning, collection, storage, cleaning, analysis, and reporting. It emphasizes ethical data collection, data quality, confidentiality, security, and sustainable storage practices The module provides hands-on training on:

Google forms for digital questionnaire design
Kobo Toolbox for mobile and field-based data collection
Microsoft Excel for cleaning, analysis, visualization, and reporting

The module strengthens practical skills in designing tools, managing submissions, validating records, and producing summaries for decision making.






TipModule Focus



Ensure that participants are able to develop digital forms, manage datasets effectively, and produce basic analytical outputs for monitoring, evaluation, and surveillance workflows.

title: Mathematical Modelling Techniques
text:
Introduction
This module focuses on infectious disease transmission modelling and its application in public health surveillance, preparedness, and outbreak response. It introduces participants to the principles of epidemic modelling, including the differences between deterministic and stochastic approaches.
Participants will explore foundational compartmental models such as SI, SIR, and SEIR, and learn how these models represent disease transmission dynamics. The module covers key epidemiological concepts including growth rate, reproduction number (R₀), herd immunity, and epidemic thresholds.
The module also demonstrates how to simulate public health interventions, including vaccination, treatment, and social distancing, while introducing key modelling processes such as parameter estimation, model calibration, scenario analysis, uncertainty assessment, and policy interpretation.






TipExpected Outcome



Participants will be able to implement and interpret basic infectious disease models in R, explore outbreak dynamics, evaluate intervention scenarios, and apply modelling results to support public health decision-making.

title: Group Project
text:
The project covers the topics of data importation, cleaning and wrangling in R among other aspects learnt in the past few days. For each project, you should try and come up with an objective and carry out descriptive analysis that helps answer your objective. If possible, you may carry out statistical analysis to answer your objective. The project code should be clearly written (with comments) and should be submitted by the group leader to the address: hathiany@abrbowatch.com by Thursday 13th November 2025.
If possible, you can use R Markdown for the project and share the .rmd file while submitting your work. Each project will be tackled by one group independently while one group will be allowed to choose a project of their choice. In case of any challenges, you may get in touch with your mentor for assistance/guidance.
Finally, to enable the group members interact, we have created WhatsApp groups where you can join and be part of the team as you work on the project. See the assignment document on the link to join and join via the ARBOWATCH WhatsApp group.

title: Introduction to R for Public Health Surveillance
text:
R and RStudio are powerful, open-source tools widely used for modern public health data analysis, enabling analysts to manage, explore, visualize, and communicate data-driven insights effectively. This module introduces participants to the R programming environment and the RStudio interface, with a focus on practical applications in public health surveillance and epidemiological analysis.
Using the tidyverse workflow, participants will learn essential data analysis processes, including importing, cleaning, transforming, summarizing, and visualizing health data. The module provides hands-on experience with key R packages such as readr, dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2 for efficient and reproducible analytical workflows.
By the end of the module, participants will be able to apply R to perform descriptive analyses, generate meaningful visualizations, interpret disease patterns and trends, and create reproducible reports that support evidence-based public health decision-making.






TipModule Focus



Develop practical R skills for managing surveillance datasets, calculating key public health indicators, creating informative visualizations, and producing reproducible analytical outputs for routine public health analysis.

title: Statistical Modelling for Public Health Research
text:
This module provides a foundation in statistical modelling for epidemiological and surveillance data analysis. It introduces key concepts in statistical inference, beginning with hypothesis formulation and testing, including p-values, confidence intervals, and commonly used statistical tests.
Participants will learn the principles of statistical modelling, including the relationship between response and explanatory variables, confounding, interaction effects, and the development of conceptual models. The module introduces essential regression approaches, including:

Linear regression for continuous outcomes
Logistic regression for binary outcomes
Poisson and Negative Binomial regression for count data

The module also covers time series methods for identifying trends, assessing seasonality, and supporting short-term forecasting of public health events.






TipExpected Outcome



Participants will be able to select appropriate statistical models, apply them in R, interpret model outputs, and communicate findings to support evidence-based public health action.

title: ARBO-WATCH Capacity Building Hub
text:
The ARBO-WATCH project seeks to design and deploy dengue and Chikungunya fever decision support tools informed by process-based models in Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia. These analyses will utilize relevant primary and secondary data from all these countries to uncover broader epidemiological patterns of these diseases in the region. The project is being implemented by a consortium made up of nine institutions including ILRI, the Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya’s Ministry of Health, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Ethiopia Public Health Institute, Global One Health Initiative, Ohio State University, Abrar University and the Ministry of Health Somalia.
Read here to learn more about the project.

title: ARBO-WATCH Capacity Building Hub
text:
JKUAT Team





Henry Athiany



Henry Athiany
Research Biostatistician
Henry Athiany is a Lecturer in the Department of Statistics and Actuarial Sciences (STACS) at JKUAT, with training in Biostatistics and Epidemiology and a background in Mathematics and Computer Science. His research spans epidemiology, infectious disease modelling, Bayesian and spatiotemporal analysis, clinical trials, statistical computing, bioinformatics, time-series forecasting, and mental health analytics. With over 15 years of experience working with large-scale eHealth and routinely collected healthcare data, he has contributed to national public health initiatives, including serving on Kenya’s COVID-19 Modelling Technical Committee and supporting multiple Ministry of Health projects on digital health systems, diagnostics optimization, and health information interoperability. He is also an experienced trainer in statistical software and research methods and has held leadership roles within the International Biometric Society and the Statistical Society of Kenya. Currently, he supports the ARBO-WATCH project as part of the JKUAT team.






Caroline Wanja Mugo



Caroline Wanja Mugo
Lecturer Biostatistics
Caroline Wanja Mugo is a Lecturer in Biostatistics at JKUAT with a background in Biostatistics and Epidemiology. Her research interests include infectious disease epidemiology, statistical methods for public health, and data-driven decision-making. She has experience working with large datasets and routinely collected healthcare data, contributing to national public health initiatives. Caroline has also been involved in training and capacity-building efforts in biostatistics and epidemiology. She currently supports the ARBO-WATCH project as part of the JKUAT team.






Anthony Waititu



Anthony Waititu
Associate Professor
Gichuhi A. Waititu is an Associate Professor of Statistics at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT), Kenya. He currently serves as the Dean of the School of Mathematics and Physical Sciences at JKUAT. He has over twenty (20) years of experience in teaching applied statistics at university level, alongside extensive engagement in research and academic leadership. His research interests focus on Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence, with applications in data science and statistical modelling.






Charity Wamwea



Charity Wamwea
Charity Wamwea is a lecturer and researcher in Actuarial Science, Applied Statistics, and Mathematical Finance at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT). She specializes in statistical, risk, and financial modelling, machine learning, and data science, with research interests spanning epidemiology, public health, survival analysis, infectious disease modelling, and non‑communicable diseases. Her work applies quantitative methods to address challenges in health systems, disease surveillance, and financial risk management.
